title: Big O: time complexity, space complexity and growth rates
learningObjectives: Explain input size, operation counting and asymptotic growth, and distinguish Big O upper bounds from exact running-time measurements.
Recognise constant, logarithmic, linear, linearithmic, quadratic and exponential growth rates and compare how they scale.
Analyse loops, nested loops, halving processes and recursive calls to estimate worst-case time complexity.
Distinguish best-case, average-case and worst-case analysis, and identify the assumptions needed for each claim.
Explain auxiliary space separately from input storage, including recursion-stack space and the effect of in-place algorithms.
Use operation counters and carefully chosen test sizes in C to compare algorithm growth without treating one timing measurement as proof.

understand.concept: Algorithm complexity describes how resource use changes as input size grows. Time complexity estimates the number of elementary operations; space complexity estimates memory use under a stated convention. Big O, written O(f(n)), gives an asymptotic upper bound: beyond some input size, the measured growth is bounded by a constant multiple of f(n). It does not mean an exact number of seconds. Common classes include O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²) and O(2ⁿ).
understand.whyItMatters: A program that works for ten values may become impractical for ten million. Complexity helps predict scalability before running large workloads and helps compare algorithm designs. It complements measurement: real performance also depends on constant factors, compiler optimisations, memory access, hardware and input distribution.
understand.analogy: Imagine checking tickets at an event. Looking up one ticket by a direct numbered seat map can take roughly the same number of steps regardless of the crowd size; checking every ticket against every other ticket grows much faster as the crowd increases.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only about growth. Real algorithms have precise input models, operation costs, best and worst cases, memory limits and implementation details. Big O alone does not tell you which program is faster for every small input.

keyTerms.definition: A measure of how much data an algorithm receives, such as the number of array elements.
How the number of operations grows with input size under a stated case and cost model.
How memory use grows with input size; auxiliary space excludes the input when that convention is stated.
An asymptotic upper bound that suppresses constant factors and lower-order terms.
A tight asymptotic bound: the growth is bounded both above and below by constant multiples of the same function.
The maximum, expected (under a specified input distribution) or minimum resource use among inputs of a given size.
Memory used by active function calls, often proportional to recursion depth.

understand.history: The O notation was introduced in mathematical analysis by Paul Bachmann and later developed by Edmund Landau in number theory. Computer scientists adopted asymptotic notation to compare algorithms independently of particular machines. The letter O refers to an order or upper-bound family, not to a literal count of operations.

explain.narrative:
Start by defining n: for an array algorithm, n usually means the number of elements. Then choose the operation being counted, such as comparisons or loop iterations. A loop that visits each element once performs O(n) work. Two independent nested loops over the same n elements may perform O(n²) work. Repeatedly halving a search interval takes O(log n) steps. A loop nested inside a loop that halves its remaining range can produce O(n log n) work. Each claim must match the actual bounds and control flow.

Asymptotic notation ignores constant factors and lower-order terms: 3n² + 5n + 8 is O(n²). Big O is an upper bound, while Big Theta expresses a tight bound when both upper and lower bounds match. State whether a claim is worst-case, average-case or best-case. For example, linear search is O(1) best case when the first item matches and O(n) worst case when the key is absent or last; its average case depends on the input distribution.

Space analysis needs a clear convention. An algorithm may use O(1) auxiliary storage while reading an input array of n elements. A recursive algorithm may use O(log n) call-stack space if its recursion depth halves the problem each time. Do not count the input as auxiliary memory unless the chosen convention explicitly includes it.

The first example counts comparisons for a nested-loop duplicate check and a linear scan. It demonstrates quadratic and linear growth directly without relying on noisy clock measurements. The second example compares iterative and recursive binary search on a sorted array. Both take O(log n) time in the worst case; the iterative version uses O(1) auxiliary space, while the recursive version uses O(log n) call-stack space. Binary search requires sorted input and a valid array length.

examples.title: Count operations in linear and quadratic algorithms
examples.explanation: has_duplicate checks every unordered pair until it finds a match. In the no-duplicate worst case, the inner loop performs (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons, which equals n(n-1)/2 and therefore grows as O(n squared). It may return early when a duplicate is found, so actual work depends on the input. contains_value checks at most n elements, giving O(n) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary space. The comparison counters make the work visible; they are not wall-clock timings. Both functions require a valid array whenever count is nonzero. The example uses a fixed, small array so its demonstration count arithmetic is safely within size_t.

examples.title: Compare iterative and recursive binary search
examples.explanation: Both functions maintain a half-open search range [low, high), where high is one past the last candidate. The midpoint uses low + (high - low) / 2 to avoid the overflow risk of (low + high) / 2. Each unsuccessful comparison discards at least half the remaining candidates, so worst-case time is O(log n). The iterative implementation uses a fixed number of local variables and therefore O(1) auxiliary space. The recursive helper makes one call per halving step, so its call-stack space is O(log n). The array must be sorted in nondecreasing order, and a nonzero count requires a valid values array. An empty range returns false without reading an element.

practise.guidedTask: For the array [4, 8, 2, 9, 5, 7], count how many pair comparisons the nested duplicate check performs when no duplicate exists. Then count the comparisons for a linear search for 7. Repeat the theoretical pair-count calculation for n = 4, 8 and 16, and explain how doubling n affects the quadratic count compared with the linear count.
practise.independentTask: Implement linear search, binary search and a nested-loop duplicate detector. Count comparisons rather than using elapsed time. Test empty input, one element, a match at the first and last positions, a missing value, duplicate values and sorted versus unsorted arrays. Write a short analysis stating each algorithm's best and worst time complexity and auxiliary space. Explain why binary search must not be used on an unsorted array.
hints: Define n before analysing an algorithm; do not leave the input-size measure ambiguous.
A single pass over n elements is O(n); two nested passes over pairs can be O(n squared).
The sum 1 + 2 + ... + (n - 1) equals n(n - 1)/2, which is Theta(n squared).
Repeatedly halving a search range gives logarithmic growth, but binary search requires sorted data.
Separate the memory occupied by the input from auxiliary storage, and include recursive call-stack use when relevant.
State best, average or worst case and the assumptions behind average-case input distributions; one timing run does not prove complexity.

questions.prompt: What does Big O notation primarily describe?
options: An asymptotic upper bound on how resource use grows with input size
The exact number of CPU seconds for every input
The number of lines in a C source file
The amount of RAM installed in a computer
questions.answer: An asymptotic upper bound on how resource use grows with input size
questions.explanation: Big O describes an upper bound on growth after ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms; it is not an exact runtime measurement.

questions.prompt: In the worst case, how many comparisons does a nested-loop check of all unordered pairs of n elements perform?
options: n(n - 1)/2, which is Theta(n squared)
Exactly n
Exactly log n
A constant independent of n
questions.explanation: The loop compares each pair once, giving (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons.

questions.prompt: Why does binary search have logarithmic worst-case time on a sorted array?
options: Each comparison discards about half of the remaining search range
It checks every element twice
It allocates a new array for every comparison
It always finds the target at index zero
questions.answer: Each comparison discards about half of the remaining search range
questions.explanation: Repeated halving reduces the candidate range geometrically, requiring O(log n) comparisons.

questions.prompt: What is the auxiliary space complexity of the iterative binary search shown in the lesson?
options: O(n)
O(n squared)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: The iterative algorithm uses a fixed number of local variables and does not allocate storage that grows with n.

questions.prompt: Which statement about average-case complexity is correct?
options: It depends on an assumed or specified distribution of inputs
It is always exactly halfway between best and worst case
It is identical to Big O for every algorithm
It can be determined from one timing measurement
questions.answer: It depends on an assumed or specified distribution of inputs
questions.explanation: Average-case analysis requires a model of how inputs are distributed; without that assumption the average is not defined.
